overview: This file brings together U.S.–Japanese diplomatic and filing records concerning plant quarantine in colonial Taiwan. Its principal documents are a December 1931 note from the Japanese Ambassador announcing amended Formosan quarantine regulations, two enclosed specimen certificates for plants inspected before export, and the State Department’s acknowledgment. Later items are a 1938 cross-reference to a report by Warner on Taiwan’s quarantine regulations and a 1939 internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs instruction that only the report’s title need be noted; a much later 1984 U.S. District Court filing stamp appears on one enclosure.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy note on amended Formosan plant-quarantine regulations
subfiles.from: Japanese Ambassador to the United States
subfiles.about: The Japanese Ambassador informs the Secretary of State that the Government of Formosa has amended its plant-quarantine regulations and supplies two new export-inspection forms.
subfiles.summary: The note announces that Forms Nos. 7 and 8 of the Certificate of Examination of Plants took effect on October 1, 1931. The Ambassador encloses copies and asks the State Department to notify the competent American authorities. Departmental annotations record acknowledgment, distribution to agriculture and commerce officials, and filing on December 15.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Form No. 7, Certificate of Examination of Plants
subfiles.about: A specimen phytosanitary certificate attests that plants have been inspected and appear free from dangerous insects and plant diseases.
subfiles.summary: Form No. 7 provides blank spaces for shipment, inspector, inspection date, issue date, and description of plants. It identifies the issuing authority as the Government Plant Quarantine Station at Taihoku, Formosa, Japan. The form was one of the new certificates reported as effective from October 1, 1931.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Form No. 8, parcel inspection certificate
subfiles.about: A specimen certificate states that plants included in a parcel were inspected and appeared free of dangerous insects and diseases.
subfiles.summary: Form No. 8 is a compact parcel certificate containing blank spaces for the parcel, inspector, inspection date, station location, and issue date. Like Form No. 7, it certifies apparent freedom from dangerous insects and plant diseases. The page also bears a much later U.S. District Court stamp from New Haven dated February 28, 1984, apparently unrelated to the original enclosure’s creation.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of the Japanese Embassy note
subfiles.to: Japanese Ambassador to the United States
subfiles.about: The Secretary of State acknowledges the Japanese note and confirms that its information and enclosures were transmitted to the appropriate U.S. authorities.
subfiles.summary: The acknowledgment identifies the incoming communication as Japanese note No. 148 of December 7, 1931. It confirms receipt of the amended Formosan plant-quarantine regulations and states that copies of the note and enclosures were forwarded to the appropriate government authorities for information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Warner’s report on Taiwan quarantine regulations
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects researchers to file 800.61211/59 for Warner’s report and copies of Taiwan’s plant-quarantine regulations.
subfiles.summary: This document does not reproduce the underlying report. It identifies a communication from Taihoku by Warner, dated December 15, 1938, concerning plant-quarantine regulations then in force in Taiwan and forwarding copies of them. The sheet directs the reader to item No. 54 in file 800.61211/59.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs instruction to note only the report title
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs file staff
subfiles.about: An internal reviewer advises that only the title of the referenced report needs to be entered in the record.
subfiles.summary: The brief internal note states that, in the writer’s opinion, only the report’s title need be noted. It is signed with the initials JMJ and bears the date November 17, 1939. Two apparent routing names, “Lee” and “Jews,” have been struck through.

interest: The file preserves both the substance and the bureaucratic handling of plant-quarantine policy in Japanese-ruled Taiwan. The two specimen certificates are useful evidence of colonial phytosanitary administration and the language used to certify export plants, while the diplomatic notes show how regulatory changes were communicated to American agriculture and commerce authorities. The 1938 cross-reference and 1939 filing instruction also reveal how the State Department distributed related material across its decimal filing system; the anomalous 1984 court stamp adds evidence of the records’ later custodial or legal history.
